questions.stem: What does „der Mauerfall“ refer to?
options: The end of the Second World War in Europe in May 1945
The opening of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989
The building of the Berlin Wall in August 1961
The reunification of Germany in October 1990
questions.explanation: „Der Fall der Mauer“ is the night the border crossings in Berlin opened, 9 November 1989. Reunification followed almost a year later, on 3 October 1990, and is a separate event.

questions.stem: What does „die Stunde Null“ refer to in German history?
options: The founding of the two separate German states in the year 1949, East and West
The first minute of German reunification on 3 October 1990
The collapse and fresh start at the end of the Second World War in 1945
The moment the Berlin Wall opened on the night of 9 November 1989
questions.explanation: „Die Stunde Null“ (zero hour) describes Germany in May 1945: defeated, in ruins and starting again. Historians debate how complete the break really was, but the term itself always refers to 1945.

questions.stem: What does „Ostalgie“ mean?
options: Nostalgia for aspects of everyday life in the former GDR
A longing to travel through the countries of Eastern Europe
Grief felt by families divided by the inner German border
The celebration of Easter traditions in eastern Germany
questions.explanation: „Ostalgie“ blends „Ost“ (east) and „Nostalgie“. It describes a fond memory of products, routines and certainties of life in the DDR, not a wish for the state itself to return.

questions.stem: What is „die Erinnerungskultur“?
options: A school subject in which pupils learn by heart
The habit of keeping family photos and diaries
A collection of folk songs passed down orally
The ways a society publicly remembers its past
questions.explanation: „Die Erinnerung“ is memory or remembrance. In Germany the term covers memorials, museums, commemorative days and school programs about the Nazi era and the GDR.

questions.stem: What does „die Vergangenheitsbewältigung“ describe?
options: Rebuilding the cities that were destroyed during the Second World War
Teaching German history only up to the year 1933
Returning property that was taken during the war
Confronting and coming to terms with a difficult past
questions.explanation: „Die Vergangenheit“ is the past and „bewältigen“ is to cope with or master. The term is used for Germany's public reckoning with the Nazi era, through memorials, education and debate.

questions.stem: „Für meine Großeltern war die Wende ein Neuanfang, aber auch ein Verlust: Ihre Fabrik wurde geschlossen, und sie mussten sich mit fünfzig ganz neu orientieren.“ What does the writer say?
options: Change had little effect on their working lives or their plans
Change forced them to move to the West straight after the Wall fell
Change brought new chances but also cost them their jobs in midlife
Change allowed them to open their own factory at the age of fifty
questions.explanation: „Ein Neuanfang, aber auch ein Verlust“ holds both sides, and the colon introduces the loss: the factory closed and at fifty they had to start again. The passage says nothing about moving west.

questions.stem: „Kafka lebte in Prag, schrieb aber auf Deutsch – ein Hinweis darauf, dass die deutschsprachige Kultur nie an die Grenzen eines Staates gebunden war.“ What does the writer conclude?
options: German-speaking writers have nearly always lived inside Germany's borders
Kafka's works first appeared in Czech before they were translated
German-language culture has never been confined to a single country
Kafka wrote in German because Prague was then a city in Germany
questions.explanation: „Nie an die Grenzen eines Staates gebunden“ means never tied to one state's borders, and Kafka writing in German in Prague is the evidence. In Kafka's lifetime Prague belonged to Austria-Hungary and then Czechoslovakia, not to Germany.

questions.stem: Gustav Klimt, painter of „Der Kuss“, is associated with which city and movement?
options: Dresden and German Romanticism
Vienna and the Vienna Secession
Berlin and the Bauhaus
Munich and the Blue Rider group
questions.explanation: Klimt helped found the Vienna Secession in 1897, breaking with the academic art of the time. „Der Blaue Reiter“ was a Munich group of the 1910s.

questions.stem: In Kafka's story „Die Verwandlung“, what happens to Gregor Samsa?
options: He is arrested one morning without being told why
He sells his soul to the devil in exchange for knowledge
He travels to America and is lost in a strange city
He wakes up one morning transformed into a huge insect
questions.explanation: „Die Verwandlung“ (The Metamorphosis) opens with Gregor already transformed. Arrest without a reason is the plot of Kafka's novel „Der Prozess“, and the pact with the devil is Goethe's „Faust“.

questions.stem: Which idea is Bertolt Brecht's „epic theatre“ known for?
options: Grand opera, with music and drama joined into one work of art
Fairytale plots, adapted from folk tales for young audiences
The alienation effect, which keeps the audience thinking critically
Total illusion, which makes the audience forget it is in a theatre
questions.explanation: Brecht's „Verfremdungseffekt“ breaks the illusion, with songs, signs and actors addressing the audience, so that spectators judge rather than simply feel. Total illusion is exactly what he rejected.

questions.stem: Whose poem „An die Freude“ did Beethoven set in his Ninth Symphony, now the melody of the European anthem?
options: Bertolt Brecht's
Friedrich Schiller's
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's
Heinrich Heine's
questions.explanation: Beethoven's final movement sets Schiller's ode, and its melody was adopted as the European anthem. Goethe and Schiller were friends in Weimar, which makes Goethe the tempting answer.

questions.stem: What was „das Wirtschaftswunder“?
options: East Germany's state-planned economy after 1949
The introduction of the euro in Germany
The rebuilding of Berlin as the capital after reunification
West Germany's rapid economic recovery in the 1950s
questions.explanation: „Das Wunder“ is a miracle: after 1948 West Germany's economy grew so fast that the recovery seemed miraculous. It is a key idea in explaining post-war West German identity.

questions.stem: In autumn 1989, protesters in Leipzig first chanted „Wir sind das Volk“; later many chanted „Wir sind ein Volk“. What did the change of one word show?
options: A shift from supporting the GDR government to opposing it
A shift from peaceful protest to calls for armed resistance
A shift from demands for freedom to travel to demands for higher wages
A shift from demanding democratic rights to demanding German unity
questions.explanation: „Das Volk“ claimed that the people, not the party, held authority; „ein Volk“ declared that East and West Germans were one nation. The slogans trace the path from reform to reunification.

questions.stem: What was „die Stasi“?
options: The West German federal border police along the inner border
The parliament of the former GDR
The East German national football team
The GDR's secret police and state security service
questions.explanation: „Stasi“ is short for „Staatssicherheit“, the Ministry for State Security, which spied on the GDR's own citizens through a vast network of informers. Its files were opened to the public after reunification.

questions.stem: What were the „Trümmerfrauen“?
options: Women who ran the first German elections after 1945
Women who cleared the rubble of bombed cities after the war
Women who worked in armaments factories during the war
Women who protested against the Berlin Wall in the 1960s
questions.explanation: „Die Trümmer“ are ruins or rubble. The image of women clearing bricks by hand became a symbol of rebuilding after 1945.

questions.stem: In 1970 the West German chancellor Willy Brandt knelt at the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. What did this „Kniefall“ come to symbolise?
options: Brandt's personal grief for German soldiers killed in Poland
Germany's acknowledgement of and atonement for Nazi crimes
West Germany's claim to the territories it had lost in 1945
The beginning of German reunification talks with Poland
questions.explanation: The gesture was widely read as asking forgiveness for the crimes of the Nazi era. It is a key moment in German „Erinnerungskultur“ (culture of remembrance).

questions.stem: Article 1 of Germany's Basic Law begins „Die Würde des Menschen ist unantastbar.“ What does it mean?
options: The will of the people is supreme
Human dignity is inviolable
Human life is short and precious
All people are born free and equal
questions.explanation: „Die Würde“ is dignity and „unantastbar“ means untouchable. Placing it first in the 1949 „Grundgesetz“ was a deliberate response to the Nazi era.

questions.stem: Around 6 January, children dressed as the Three Kings go from house to house. Who are they?
options: „Die Sternsinger“, who collect for charity and chalk a blessing on the door
„Die Krampusse“, who frighten children who have misbehaved during the year
„Die Narren“, who open the carnival season with costumes and songs
„Die Laternenkinder“, who sing for sweets on the evening of St Martin's Day
questions.explanation: „Sternsinger“ (star singers) follow a star on a pole, sing, collect money for children's charities and write C+M+B with the year above the door. Krampus belongs to early December and the „Narren“ to carnival.

questions.stem: „In Köln heißt es Karneval, in Mainz Fastnacht und in München Fasching.“ What does this sentence show?
options: One festival has different names in different regions
Three separate festivals are held in three different cities
Each city celebrates its carnival in a different season
The carnival is celebrated only in these three cities
questions.explanation: The pre-Lent carnival is one tradition with regional names. Recognising regional variation like this is part of studying lifestyles in German-speaking communities.

questions.stem: What is „ein Richtfest“?
options: A court hearing held in the town square in the Middle Ages
A harvest festival held when the grapes have been picked
A family party held when a young person reaches the age of eighteen
A celebration held when the roof frame of a new building is finished
questions.explanation: At a „Richtfest“ a small tree or wreath is placed on the finished roof frame and the builders are thanked. It is a custom from the building trades still held today.

questions.stem: What is „der Almabtrieb“?
options: A ski race down an Alpine meadow at the end of winter
Bringing decorated cattle down from the Alpine pastures in autumn
Driving cattle up to the Alpine pastures at the start of spring
A cheese market held in Alpine villages each summer
questions.explanation: „Die Alm“ is a high mountain pasture and „abtreiben“ here means to drive down. When the summer has passed safely, the cows return to the valley wearing flowers and bells.

questions.stem: What is „die Tracht“?
options: A style of wooden farmhouse found in the Alpine valleys
Traditional regional costume, such as the Dirndl or Lederhosen
A traditional regional dish, such as Weißwurst, Knödel or Brezeln
A traditional folk dance performed at village festivals
questions.explanation: „Die Tracht“ is regional dress, worn for festivals and special occasions, especially in Bavaria and Austria. It is a cultural product that shows regional identity.

questions.stem: Which are the four national languages of Switzerland?
options: German, French, Italian and English
German, French, Dutch and Romansh
German, French, Italian and Romansh
German, French and Italian only
questions.explanation: Switzerland has four national languages, and German is spoken by the majority. Romansh, spoken in Graubünden, is the one most often forgotten.

questions.stem: In which group is German an official language in every country listed?
options: Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Poland and the Czech Republic
Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Sweden, Luxembourg, Belgium and Norway
Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg and Belgium
Germany, Austria, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Denmark
questions.explanation: German is official in Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg and Belgium: in Belgium only in the east, and in Switzerland and Luxembourg alongside other languages. Dutch is the language of the Netherlands, a close relative but a separate language.

questions.stem: What is „Plattdeutsch“?
options: A form of German used only in written legal documents
The German dialect spoken in Austria and Bavaria
Low German, a regional language of northern Germany
The flat, unaccented German of television news
questions.explanation: Low German („Niederdeutsch“) is distinct from standard High German and is still spoken and sung in coastal regions. It is recognised as a regional language.

questions.stem: An Austrian talks about „Paradeiser“ and „Erdäpfel“. What would someone from Hamburg usually call them?
options: „Tomaten“ and „Äpfel“
„Paprika“ and „Rüben“
„Tomaten“ and „Kartoffeln“
„Pflaumen“ and „Kartoffeln“
questions.explanation: Austrian German has its own words for many foods: „Paradeiser“ are tomatoes and „Erdäpfel“ (earth apples) are potatoes. Reading „Erdäpfel“ as plain apples is the trap.

questions.stem: How do German-speaking Swiss typically use dialect and standard German?
options: Dialect in writing; standard German only when speaking
Standard German everywhere; dialect only among the elderly
Dialect for most everyday speech; standard German mainly for writing
Standard German at home and with friends; dialect only for official speeches
questions.explanation: Swiss German dialects are spoken by all generations, even in many formal settings, while written texts are mostly in Swiss Standard German. This split between spoken and written forms is unusual in the German-speaking world.

questions.stem: In Austria, what does „Jänner“ mean?
options: January
June
July
Yesterday
questions.explanation: Austrians say „Jänner“ where Germans say „Januar“. The study design asks students to know that different national standards of German exist.

questions.stem: Why do many Germans watch the English sketch „Dinner for One“ every year?
options: It is shown in schools to teach English
It is screened at every Christmas market
It opens the carnival season each November
It is a New Year's Eve television tradition
questions.explanation: The black-and-white sketch is broadcast every „Silvester“ and has become part of the evening, even though it is little known in Britain. It shows how a cultural product can take on new meaning in another culture.

questions.stem: What is „das Schützenfest“?
options: A festival held by a local marksmen's club, with a shooting contest
A celebration of the local fire brigade's founding anniversary
A festival at which hunters show the game they have shot
A memorial day for the soldiers who died protecting the town long ago
questions.explanation: The „Schützenverein“ holds a contest, crowns a „Schützenkönig“ and hosts a parade and fair. It is one of the oldest forms of German club life.

questions.stem: What is „ein Verein“?
options: A registered club or association, such as a sports or choir club
A council-run leisure centre that is open to the whole public
An informal group of friends who meet now and then at a café or pub
A company that organises group holidays for its members
questions.explanation: German community life is built around „Vereine“: sports clubs, choirs, shooting clubs and volunteer fire brigades. A Verein has members, a committee and rules, which makes it more formal than a group of friends.

questions.stem: Which languages are official in Luxembourg?
options: Luxembourgish, French and German
Luxembourgish and Dutch only
French, Italian and German
German and English only
questions.explanation: Luxembourg has three official languages, and many residents move between them daily. German is widely used in the press and in schools.

questions.stem: Where is South Tyrol, where German is an official language?
options: In southern Switzerland
In eastern France
In northern Italy
In western Austria
questions.explanation: South Tyrol („Südtirol“) became part of Italy after the First World War, and most of its people still speak German. It is one of the places the study design lists where German is official.

questions.stem: Who was Ferdinand von Mueller?
options: A German-born botanist who directed Melbourne's Botanic Gardens
A Prussian explorer who vanished crossing Australia in 1848
A Lutheran pastor who led settlers to the Barossa Valley
A winemaker who planted some of the first vineyards in South Australia
questions.explanation: Von Mueller became Victoria's government botanist and named thousands of Australian plants. The explorer who disappeared in 1848 was Ludwig Leichhardt.

questions.stem: What does „Multikulti“ mean in everyday German?
options: A shop that sells goods from many countries
A person who speaks many languages fluently
A festival with food from many countries
Multiculturalism, a society of many cultures
questions.explanation: „Multikulti“ is a colloquial short form of „multikulturell“. It can be neutral or ironic depending on the speaker, which is worth noticing in a text.

questions.stem: „Viele Gastarbeiter blieben länger als geplant. Ihre Enkel sind fester Teil der Gesellschaft, fühlen sich aber manchmal weder hier noch dort ganz zu Hause.“ What point is made?
options: Later generations belong yet can feel not fully at home anywhere
Most guest workers returned home after a few years, as planned
Their grandchildren feel at home only in their grandparents' country
Their families have been unable to find secure work in Germany
questions.explanation: „Weder hier noch dort“ means neither here nor there, so the grandchildren do not feel completely at home in either place. „Länger als geplant“ rules out the reading that they went home.

questions.stem: Which sentence presents a personal perspective rather than a fact?
options: „Für mich ist der Weihnachtsmarkt das Schönste am ganzen Jahr.“
„Den Dresdner Striezelmarkt gibt es seit dem 15. Jahrhundert.“
„Viele Weihnachtsmärkte öffnen schon Ende November.“
„Auf dem Markt werden Glühwein und Lebkuchen verkauft.“
questions.explanation: „Für mich“ and the superlative „das Schönste“ signal a personal judgement. The key skills ask students to distinguish factual information from personal perspectives; the Dresden date is a checkable fact.

questions.stem: In the Unit 4 interview the assessor asks: „Wie hat sich dieser Brauch im Laufe der Zeit verändert?“ What are you being asked?
options: Where the custom is still practised
What you personally like about it
How the custom has changed over time
Why you chose to research this custom
questions.explanation: „Im Laufe der Zeit“ means over the course of time and „sich verändern“ is to change. Comparing the past and the present is exactly what the study design asks students to be ready to discuss.

questions.stem: The assessor asks: „Inwiefern spiegelt dieses Fest die Werte der Gemeinschaft wider?“ What does the question want?
options: To what extent the festival reflects the community's values
When the community first began to hold the festival
Which members of the community organise the festival
How the festival differs from a similar one held in Australia
questions.explanation: „Inwiefern“ asks to what extent, and „widerspiegeln“ is to reflect. Recognising these question words lets a student give an analytical answer rather than a description.

questions.stem: „Der Brauch ist heute eher ein Touristenmagnet als ein religiöses Fest.“ What does the speaker claim?
options: The custom has lost its tourists since it became mainly religious
The custom is equally a tourist event and a religious occasion
The custom was invented to attract more tourists to a small religious town
The custom now draws tourists more than it serves a religious purpose
questions.explanation: „Eher A als B“ means more A than B, so the tourist side now outweighs the religious one. Reading it as 'equally' misses that „eher … als“ ranks the two.
